title: Nucleophiles, heterolytic fission and nucleophilic substitution
html:
Guiding question

What happens when reactants share electron pairs with others?

Most organic (and many inorganic) reactions happen because an electron-rich species donates a pair of electrons to an electron-poor species, forming a new covalent bond. The donor is a nucleophile (Lewis base); the acceptor is an electrophile (Lewis acid). In mechanisms, the movement of an electron pair is shown by a double-headed curly arrow, which must start at the electrons (a lone pair, a negative charge or a bond) and end where the new bond forms or where the electrons end up.

CodeUnderstanding
R3.4.1A nucleophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the electrophile) by donating both bonding electrons.
R3.4.2In a nucleophilic substitution reaction, a nucleophile replaces a leaving group.
R3.4.3Heterolytic fission is the breakage of a covalent bond when both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments.
R3.4.4An electrophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the nucleophile) by accepting both bonding electrons.
R3.4.5Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the C=C double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
R3.4.6 AHLA Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor.
R3.4.7 AHLWhen a Lewis base reacts with a Lewis acid, a coordination bond is formed. Nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids.
R3.4.8 AHLCoordination bonds are formed when ligands donate an electron pair to transition element cations, forming complex ions.
R3.4.9 AHLNucleophilic substitution reactions include the SN1 and SN2 mechanisms.
R3.4.10 AHLThe rate of the substitution reactions is influenced by the identity of the leaving group.
R3.4.11 AHLAlkenes readily undergo electrophilic addition reactions (mechanisms).
R3.4.12 AHLThe relative stability of carbocations in the addition reactions between hydrogen halides and unsymmetrical alkenes can be used to explain the reaction mechanism (Markovnikov).
R3.4.13 AHLElectrophilic substitution reactions include the reactions of benzene with electrophiles.
Do now: name these halogenoalkanes, classify them, and predict which has the highest boiling point: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane

1-bromobutane is primary, 2-bromobutane secondary, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane tertiary (all C₄H₉Br). The straight-chain 1-bromobutane has the highest boiling point: its molecules have the largest contact area, so the London (dispersion) forces between them are strongest. Branching makes molecules more compact and lowers the boiling point.

R3.4.1 Nucleophiles

DefinitionA nucleophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the electrophile) by donating both bonding electrons. Every nucleophile must have a lone pair of electrons.

"Nucleophile" means "nucleus-loving": nucleophiles are attracted to positive or partially positive (δ+) centres, especially electron-deficient carbon atoms. Nucleophiles can be:

  • Negatively charged: hydroxide :OH⁻, cyanide :CN⁻, halide ions (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻), alkoxide RO⁻, hydride H⁻
  • Neutral, with a lone pair: water H₂O:, ammonia :NH₃, amines RNH₂, alcohols ROH

Why is OH⁻ a better nucleophile than H₂O? Both have lone pairs on oxygen, but the hydroxide ion carries a full negative charge, so it is more strongly attracted to the δ+ carbon and its lone pair is more available. Water has only a δ− on oxygen, so reactions with water are much slower.

Common mistakeA nucleophile does not have to be negatively charged (NH₃ and H₂O are neutral nucleophiles). The essential feature is the lone pair. In MCQs, "What must be present on a nucleophile?" → a lone pair of electrons.

Which species cannot act as a nucleophile?

  1. NH₃
  2. CN⁻
  3. CH₄
  4. H₂O

Methane has no lone pair: all four electron pairs on C are bonding pairs. The others all have at least one lone pair to donate.

R3.4.3 Heterolytic fission

DefinitionHeterolytic fission is the breaking of a covalent bond in which both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments, forming a cation and an anion.

The electrons go to the more electronegative atom. It is shown by a single double-headed curly arrow from the middle of the bond to the atom that keeps the pair.

H–Br → H⁺ + Br⁻
(CH₃)₃C–Br → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻

Compare homolytic fission (R3.3), where each atom keeps one electron and two radicals form. Heterolytic fission happens in polar bonds, often helped by a polar solvent, and is the bond-breaking step in nucleophilic substitution and electrophilic addition.

In heterolytic fission both electrons go to one fragment, giving ions; in homolytic fission each atom keeps one electron, giving radicals.

R3.4.2 Nucleophilic substitution of halogenoalkanes

In a nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile replaces a leaving group. In halogenoalkanes the leaving group is a halide ion.

Why are halogenoalkanes attacked by nucleophiles? Halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar: Cδ+–Xδ−. The δ+ carbon attracts the lone pair of a nucleophile. Halogenoalkanes are also more reactive than alkanes because the C–X bond (especially C–Br and C–I) is weaker than a C–H bond.

The general steps:

  1. The nucleophile is attracted to the δ+ carbon of the C–X bond. Its lone pair moves towards the carbon (curly arrow from the lone pair or negative charge on the nucleophile to the carbon).
  2. As the nucleophile approaches, the electrons in the C–X bond are repelled towards the halogen.
  3. A new C–Nu bond forms and the C–X bond breaks heterolytically: both electrons go to the halogen, which leaves as a halide ion (curly arrow from the C–X bond to X).
NucleophileReagent and conditionsProductExample equation
OH⁻NaOH or KOH, aqueous, warm (heat under reflux)AlcoholCH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻
CN⁻KCN in ethanol, warmNitrile (chain + 1 carbon)CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN + Br⁻
NH₃Excess concentrated NH₃ in ethanol, heated in a sealed tubeAmineCH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br
  • Cyanide is useful in synthesis because it lengthens the carbon chain by one, and the –CN group can be converted into other groups such as –COOH.
  • Ammonia reacts in a 2 : 1 ratio: the first NH₃ substitutes, and a second NH₃ removes H⁺ from the intermediate to give the neutral amine and NH₄⁺. Excess ammonia is used so that the amine product does not itself react with more halogenoalkane (forming secondary amines).
Worked exampleDescribing the mechanism in words. Bromoethane reacts with warm aqueous sodium hydroxide. Describe the mechanism.
Equation: CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻ (or + NaOH → … + NaBr)
Arrow 1: from a lone pair on the O of OH⁻ to the δ+ carbon bonded to Br.
Arrow 2: from the C–Br bond to the Br atom.
Products: ethanol and a bromide ion, Br⁻.
Marking points: arrow must start on the lone pair/negative charge of O (not on H); arrow showing Br leaving; correct products including Br⁻.
Your turn: describe the mechanism of 2-chloropropane with aqueous hydroxide ions.

CH₃CHClCH₃ + OH⁻ → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + Cl⁻. Curly arrow from a lone pair on O of OH⁻ to the δ+ carbon bonded to Cl (the middle carbon); curly arrow from the C–Cl bond to Cl. Products: propan-2-ol and Cl⁻.

Exam tipThe halogenoalkane classification matters (and is needed for AHL). Primary: the C bearing X is bonded to one other C (e.g. 1-bromopropane); secondary: two other C (2-chloropropane); tertiary: three other C (2-bromo-2-methylpropane). A typical SL question: "Classify 1-bromopropane, giving a reason" → primary, because the carbon bonded to Br is bonded to only one other carbon (two H atoms).

Which reagent converts 1-bromopropane into butanenitrile?

  1. NaOH(aq)
  2. KCN in ethanol
  3. excess NH₃ in ethanol
  4. HCN(g)

CN⁻ replaces Br⁻ and adds one carbon: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CN (butanenitrile, four carbons) + Br⁻.

title: Electrophiles and electrophilic addition to alkenes
html:
R3.4.4 Electrophiles

DefinitionAn electrophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the nucleophile) by accepting both bonding electrons from that partner.

Electrophiles ("electron-loving") are electron-deficient. They are usually:

  • Positively charged: H⁺ (H₃O⁺), NO₂⁺ (nitronium ion), carbocations such as CH₃CH⁺CH₃, metal ions such as Cu²⁺
  • Neutral with a δ+ atom: H in H–Br (Hδ+–Brδ−), the δ+ carbon in a halogenoalkane, carbonyl or CO₂
  • Neutral with an incomplete octet: BF₃, AlCl₃
  • Polarisable molecules in which a dipole is induced: Br₂, Cl₂ near a C=C bond

Note that in nucleophilic substitution the halogenoalkane is the electrophile, and in electrophilic addition the alkene is the nucleophile. Every one of these reactions has one of each.

Which species is an electrophile?

  1. NH₃
  2. Cl⁻
  3. NO₂⁺
  4. CH₃OH

NO₂⁺ is positively charged and electron-deficient, so it accepts an electron pair. The other three have lone pairs and act as nucleophiles.

R3.4.5 Electrophilic addition to alkenes

Alkenes are hydrocarbons with general formula CₙH₂ₙ (non-cyclic), containing a C=C double bond. The arrangement around the C=C is planar with bond angles of about 120°. Their boiling points rise with chain length (more London forces), and they are non-polar, so immiscible with water.

Alkenes contain a C=C double bond made of a σ bond and a π bond. The σ bond forms by end-on overlap of orbitals along the line between the nuclei; the π bond forms by sideways overlap of two parallel 2p orbitals, which is only possible if the molecule is planar – so rotation about C=C is restricted (the origin of E/Z isomers). The π electrons lie above and below the plane of the molecule, are less tightly held than σ electrons, and create a region of high electron density. This attracts electrophiles. The π bond is also weaker than the σ bond, so it breaks easily and the two carbons each gain a new atom: an addition reaction. Alkenes are unsaturated; addition makes them saturated.

ReagentConditionsProductEquation (ethene)
Hydrogen halide, HX (HBr, HCl, HI)Room temperatureHalogenoalkaneC₂H₄ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br
Halogen, X₂ (Br₂, Cl₂)Room temperature, in the dark; no UV or catalyst neededDihalogenoalkaneC₂H₄ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br (1,2-dibromoethane)
Water (steam), H₂OConcentrated H₃PO₄ (or H₂SO₄) catalyst, ~300 °C, 60–70 atmAlcoholC₂H₄ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH
Hydrogen, H₂ (hydrogenation)Ni catalyst, ~150 °C (or Pt/Pd at room temp)AlkaneC₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆

Hydrogenation is a reduction (R3.2) rather than an electrophilic addition, but it is an addition reaction of alkenes that you should know alongside the others.

Key pointTest for unsaturation: add bromine water (orange/brown). An alkene decolourises it quickly at room temperature, even in the dark, because the bromine adds across C=C and molecular Br₂ is used up. An alkane does not decolourise it in the dark. Write "orange to colourless", never "clear".
Worked examplePredicting products. (a) Hex-3-ene + steam → hexan-3-ol (symmetrical alkene, so only one product).
(b) Propene + Br₂ → CH₃CHBrCH₂Br (1,2-dibromopropane): one Br adds to each carbon of the old double bond.
(c) But-2-ene + HBr → CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₃ (2-bromobutane): only one product because but-2-ene is symmetrical.
(d) Which reaction gives only butan-2-ol? Adding water to but-2-ene (symmetrical). Adding water to but-1-ene gives a mixture of butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol.
Common mistakeDo not confuse the two reactions with halogens. Alkane + Br₂: free-radical substitution, needs UV light, gives HBr as a by-product (R3.3). Alkene + Br₂: electrophilic addition, happens in the dark, gives a single dibromo product and no HBr.

What is the mechanism of the reaction between propene and iodine in the dark?

  1. electrophilic addition
  2. electrophilic substitution
  3. free-radical substitution
  4. nucleophilic substitution

Halogens add across C=C without UV light; I₂ is polarized by the π electrons and acts as the electrophile.

What is the product of but-2-ene with hydrogen bromide?

  1. 1-bromobutane
  2. 2-bromobutane
  3. 2,3-dibromobutane
  4. 1,2-dibromobutane

H adds to one carbon of the C=C and Br to the other: CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₃. Because but-2-ene is symmetrical, there is only one product.

The C=C double bond has a high electron density, so it is attacked by electrophiles.

title: Lewis acids and bases, coordination bonds and complex ions (AHL)
html:
R3.4.6 Lewis acids and bases AHL

Do now: write definitions for Lewis and Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases, nucleophile and electrophile. What do you notice?

B–L acid: proton donor; B–L base: proton acceptor. Lewis acid: electron-pair acceptor; Lewis base: electron-pair donor. Nucleophile: donates an electron pair; electrophile: accepts one. So a nucleophile is a Lewis base and an electrophile is a Lewis acid, and a B–L base must be a Lewis base because it uses a lone pair to accept H⁺.

DefinitionA Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor. A Lewis base is an electron-pair donor.

Lewis theory is broader than Brønsted–Lowry theory (proton donor/acceptor, R3.1). Every Brønsted–Lowry base is a Lewis base, because accepting H⁺ requires a lone pair to bond to it. But many Lewis acids contain no hydrogen at all and so cannot be Brønsted–Lowry acids.

ReactionLewis acid (accepts pair)Lewis base (donates pair)
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺H⁺NH₃
BF₃ + NH₃ → F₃B–NH₃BF₃ (B has only 6 valence electrons)NH₃
AlCl₃ + Cl⁻ → AlCl₄⁻AlCl₃Cl⁻
Cu²⁺ + 6H₂O → [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺Cu²⁺H₂O
CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻CH₃Br (the δ+ carbon)OH⁻
CO₂ + OH⁻ → HCO₃⁻CO₂OH⁻
Exam tip"Which is a Lewis acid but not a Brønsted–Lowry acid?" Look for a species with an empty orbital or incomplete octet and no ionisable H: AlCl₃, BF₃, metal cations (Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺). HF and CH₃COOH are both (they donate H⁺); CCl₄ is neither.
"Why is NaOH both a Brønsted–Lowry and a Lewis base?" OH⁻ accepts a proton (B–L base) and does so by donating its lone pair (Lewis base/nucleophile).

Which species is a Lewis acid but not a Brønsted–Lowry acid?

  1. HCl
  2. CH₃COOH
  3. BF₃
  4. NH₄⁺

BF₃ has an incomplete octet on B and accepts an electron pair, but it has no H⁺ to donate. The other three can donate a proton (so they are both).

R3.4.7 Coordination bonds; nucleophiles are Lewis bases AHL

When a Lewis base reacts with a Lewis acid, the base supplies both electrons of the new bond. This is a coordination (dative covalent) bond, drawn as an arrow from donor to acceptor (e.g. N→B in F₃B←NH₃). Once formed, it is identical to any other covalent bond (all four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are the same).

Key pointNucleophiles are Lewis bases; electrophiles are Lewis acids. The Lewis acid–base idea links all the mechanisms in this topic: in every curly-arrow step that forms a bond, an electron pair moves from a Lewis base (nucleophile) to a Lewis acid (electrophile).

When drawing Lewis formulas to show coordination bond formation, show the lone pair on the donor atom (e.g. the N of NH₃), the empty orbital/incomplete octet on the acceptor (e.g. 6 electrons around B in BF₃), and then the product with the new bond and any formal charges (N⁺ and B⁻ in H₃N–BF₃).

R3.4.8 Complex ions and ligands AHL

Transition element cations are small, highly charged and have empty low-energy orbitals (3d, 4s, 4p), so they act as Lewis acids. Molecules or ions with lone pairs bond to them.

  • A ligand is a molecule or ion that donates a lone pair to a central metal ion, forming a coordination bond. Ligands are Lewis bases.
  • A complex ion is a central metal ion surrounded by coordinately bonded ligands.
  • The coordination number is the number of coordination bonds to the central ion (commonly 6, giving an octahedral shape with 90° bond angles; also 4, tetrahedral or square planar; and 2, linear).
Ligand typeDefinitionExamples
MonodentateDonates one lone pairH₂O, NH₃, OH⁻, CN⁻, Cl⁻
BidentateDonates two lone pairs from two atomsEthane-1,2-diamine (en), H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂; ethanedioate C₂O₄²⁻
PolydentateDonates several lone pairsEDTA⁴⁻ (six donor atoms), used to remove toxic metal ions such as Pb²⁺ from the blood

Small ligands such as H₂O and NH₃ usually give six-coordinate octahedral complexes. Larger ligands such as Cl⁻ often give four-coordinate tetrahedral complexes, e.g. [CuCl₄]²⁻. Cisplatin, [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], is square planar; Tollens' reagent, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, is linear.

charge on complex = oxidation state of metal + sum of ligand charges
Worked exampleCharges and oxidation states. (a) Charge on the complex formed from Fe³⁺ and six H₂O: +3 + 6(0) = 3+, [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺.
(b) Charge on the complex formed from Fe³⁺ and six CN⁻: +3 + 6(−1) = 3−, [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻.
(c) Oxidation state of Co in [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺: x + 5(0) + (−1) = +2, so x = +3. (So in the past-paper MCQ, "Co has oxidation number +II" is false; Co³⁺ acts as a Lewis acid and the octahedral complex has 90° angles.)
(d) Oxidation state of Pt in cisplatin, [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]: x + 0 + 2(−1) = 0, so x = +2.
(e) Cu²⁺ with six H₂O gives 2+; Cu²⁺ with four H₂O and two OH⁻ gives a neutral complex.

What is the oxidation state of iron in [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ (C₂O₄²⁻ = ethanedioate)?

x + 3(−2) = −3, so x = +3. Each bidentate ethanedioate uses two positions, so the coordination number is 6 (octahedral).

What is the coordination number of the metal in [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺?

Each en is bidentate (2 × 2 = 4 bonds) plus 2 Cl⁻: 6 coordination bonds, octahedral. Oxidation state: x + 0 + 2(−1) = +1, x = +3.
Sketch and describe: [Ag(CN)₂]⁻, [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺, [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]
ComplexShapeBond angleMetal oxidation stateCoordination number
[Ag(CN)₂]⁻linear180°+12
[Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺octahedral90°+36
[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]square planar90°+24

In the complex ion [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺, what are the oxidation state of copper and the coordination number?

  1. +2 and 4
  2. +2 and 6
  3. +4 and 6
  4. 0 and 6

NH₃ and H₂O are neutral, so Cu = +2. Four plus two monodentate ligands make six coordination bonds (octahedral).

The colour and d-orbital splitting of complexes are covered in Structure 3.1 (AHL).

title: SN1 and SN2 mechanisms and the leaving group (AHL)
html:
R3.4.9 SN1 and SN2 mechanisms AHL

At HL you must distinguish two mechanisms for nucleophilic substitution. The name tells you the key facts: S = substitution, N = nucleophilic, 1 or 2 = the molecularity of the rate-determining step (one or two species involved). In SN1 one species breaks apart first and the nucleophile adds afterwards (two steps); in SN2 the nucleophile arrives as the leaving group departs (one step).

SN2: primary halogenoalkanes (one step, bimolecular) AHL

  1. The nucleophile (e.g. OH⁻) approaches the δ+ carbon from the side opposite to the halogen ("backside attack"), because the large, electron-rich halogen blocks the front.
  2. A curly arrow goes from the lone pair on O to the carbon; at the same time a curly arrow goes from the C–Br bond to Br.
  3. An unstable transition state forms in which the carbon is partially bonded to both the incoming OH and the leaving Br (five groups around carbon, the three other groups flattened into a plane). It is drawn in square brackets with dashed partial bonds HO···C···Br and an overall negative charge: [HO···CH₂R···Br]⁻.
  4. The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically; Br⁻ leaves and the alcohol forms. The other three groups flip over like an umbrella turning inside out: inversion of configuration.
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → [HO···CH₂(C₂H₅)···Br]⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻
rate = k[halogenoalkane][OH⁻]   (second order overall)

SN2 is stereospecific: if the carbon is chiral, one enantiomer gives a single enantiomer of product with the inverted configuration. Primary halogenoalkanes use SN2 because the carbon is not crowded (little steric hindrance), and a primary carbocation would be too unstable to form.

SN1: tertiary halogenoalkanes (two steps, unimolecular) AHL

  1. Step 1 (slow, rate-determining): the C–X bond breaks heterolytically on its own (curly arrow from C–Br bond to Br), forming a carbocation intermediate and a halide ion: (CH₃)₃CBr → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻.
  2. Step 2 (fast): the nucleophile attacks the positive carbon (curly arrow from the lone pair on OH⁻ to C⁺): (CH₃)₃C⁺ + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃COH.
rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]   (first order; the nucleophile does not appear)

Tertiary halogenoalkanes use SN1 because (i) the three alkyl groups push electron density towards the positive carbon (positive inductive effect), stabilising the tertiary carbocation, and (ii) the bulky groups block backside attack (steric hindrance), so SN2 is difficult. The carbocation is trigonal planar, so the nucleophile can attack equally from either face: a chiral starting material gives a racemic mixture (50 : 50) of enantiomers. Secondary halogenoalkanes can react by either route. Because the nucleophile is not involved in the slow step, even weak nucleophiles work well in SN1.

SN1SN2
Typical substrateTertiary (3°)Primary (1°)
Number of stepsTwoOne (concerted)
Species formedCarbocation intermediate (a real, if short-lived, species)Transition state (energy maximum, cannot be isolated)
Rate equationrate = k[RX]rate = k[RX][Nu⁻]
Molecularity of RDSUnimolecularBimolecular
StereochemistryRacemic mixture (attack from both sides of planar C⁺)Inversion of configuration (stereospecific)
Energy profileTwo humps with a dip (intermediate) between; first hump higherOne hump (transition state)
Favoured byPolar protic solvents (water, alcohols)Polar aprotic solvents (propanone, DMSO)

Protic solvents have H bonded to O or N and can donate H⁺; they stabilise the carbocation and the leaving halide ion, so they favour SN1. Polar aprotic solvents (propanone, dimethyl sulfoxide, DMF, acetonitrile) do not solvate the nucleophile strongly, leaving it more reactive, so they favour SN2. These solvent effects are background only: the IB guide states the role of the solvent will not be assessed.

Worked exampleUsing rate data. Initial-rate data for C₄H₉Br + OH⁻ → C₄H₉OH + Br⁻: doubling [C₄H₉Br] doubles the rate; doubling [OH⁻] leaves the rate unchanged.
Step 1: first order in C₄H₉Br, zero order in OH⁻ → rate = k[C₄H₉Br].
Step 2: only the halogenoalkane is in the rate-determining step → SN1.
Step 3: SN1 is typical of tertiary halogenoalkanes, so C₄H₉Br is probably 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, not a primary isomer.
Worked exampleFull SN2 marking points. Explain the mechanism of 1-bromobutane with NaOH(aq).
M1: curly arrow from the lone pair/negative charge on O of OH⁻ to the C bonded to Br.
M2: curly arrow from the C–Br bond to Br.
M3: transition state in square brackets, with partial (dashed) bonds HO···C···Br and an overall negative charge.
Product: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻.
Lost marks: arrow starting on H of OH⁻; drawing a full O–C bond in the transition state; using the tertiary isomer (only 2 max).

Reaction A: CH₃I + CH₃S⁻ (SN2). Reaction B: (CH₃)₃CBr + CH₃SH (SN1). What happens to each rate if [nucleophile] is doubled?

  1. Both double
  2. A doubles, B unchanged
  3. A unchanged, B doubles
  4. Neither changes

SN2: rate = k[CH₃I][CH₃S⁻], so doubling the nucleophile doubles the rate. SN1: rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]; the nucleophile only enters the fast second step.

2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with cyanide ions. Which statement is correct?

  1. It reacts by SN2 with inversion
  2. It forms a carbocation intermediate in the rate-determining step
  3. Rate = k[RBr][CN⁻]
  4. It forms a pentavalent transition state as its only step

It is tertiary: the C–Br bond breaks first (slow) to give (CH₃)₃C⁺, which is then attacked by CN⁻ to form 2,2-dimethylpropanenitrile.

R3.4.10 Relative rates of substitution AHL

Effect of the halogen (leaving group). The rate depends mainly on the strength of the C–X bond, not on its polarity. Going down group 17 the bond gets longer and weaker, so it breaks more easily and the halide is a better leaving group:

BondC–FC–ClC–BrC–I
Bond enthalpy / kJ mol⁻¹ (data booklet)492324285228
Relative rate of substitutionslowest→→fastest

Rate: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F. Note the C–F bond is the most polar but reacts the slowest, which proves that bond strength wins over polarity. Always use the bond enthalpies in your data booklet.

Effect of the class of halogenoalkane. For the same halogen, tertiary halogenoalkanes generally react fastest (SN1 via a stable tertiary carbocation) and primary ones slowest; secondary are in between.

Exam tip"Outline how bond polarity changes down group 17" → polarity decreases because electronegativity of the halogen decreases. "Explain the trend in rate" → rate increases because C–X bond enthalpy decreases. Keep these two separate.

Which halogenoalkane reacts fastest with aqueous NaOH under the same conditions?

  1. 1-fluorobutane
  2. 1-chlorobutane
  3. 1-bromobutane
  4. 1-iodobutane

C–I (228 kJ mol⁻¹) is the weakest carbon–halogen bond, so iodide is the best leaving group – even though C–I is the least polar.

Nucleophiles are electron-pair donors and form new covalent bonds; iodoalkanes undergo substitution fastest because the C–I bond is the weakest.

title: Electrophilic addition mechanisms and Markovnikov's rule (AHL)
html:
R3.4.11 Mechanisms of electrophilic addition AHL

The mechanisms are not assessed at SL, but they help explain the products. At HL you need them for symmetrical alkenes with hydrogen halides, halogens and water.

Do now: explain why E/Z isomers form in alkenes but not in alkanes.

The π bond forms by sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the C=C axis. Rotating one carbon would break that overlap, so rotation about C=C is restricted. If each carbon of the double bond carries two different groups, the groups can be fixed on the same side (Z) or opposite sides (E). C–C single bonds (σ only) rotate freely, so alkanes have no such isomers.

Ethene + hydrogen bromide AHL

H–Br is polar (Hδ+–Brδ−), so the H end is the electrophile.

  1. Step 1: a curly arrow goes from the C=C π bond to the δ+ H of HBr; at the same time a curly arrow goes from the H–Br bond to Br. The H–Br bond breaks heterolytically. A carbocation (CH₃CH₂⁺) and a bromide ion form.
  2. Step 2: the bromide ion, now acting as a nucleophile, donates a lone pair to the positive carbon (curly arrow from lone pair/negative charge on Br⁻ to C⁺).
CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂⁺ + Br⁻ → CH₃CH₂Br

Ethene + bromine AHL

Br₂ is non-polar, so why is it an electrophile? As a Br₂ molecule approaches the electron-rich π bond, the π electrons repel the electron pair in the Br–Br bond, pushing it towards the far Br atom. This induces a dipole: Brδ+–Brδ−, with the near Br δ+.

  1. Step 1: curly arrow from the C=C π bond to the δ+ Br; curly arrow from the Br–Br bond to the far Br. A carbocation CH₂Br–CH₂⁺ and Br⁻ form. (A cyclic bromonium ion is a more accurate picture, but the carbocation version is accepted by IB.)
  2. Step 2: Br⁻ attacks the carbocation: curly arrow from Br⁻ lone pair to C⁺, giving CH₂BrCH₂Br (1,2-dibromoethane).

Ethene + water (acid-catalysed hydration) AHL

  1. Step 1: the π bond attacks H⁺ (from H₃O⁺ of the acid catalyst), forming the carbocation CH₃CH₂⁺.
  2. Step 2: a water molecule uses a lone pair on O to bond to C⁺, giving the protonated alcohol CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺.
  3. Step 3: this loses H⁺ (to another water molecule), giving ethanol and regenerating the H⁺ catalyst.
Exam tipCurly arrows in step 1 must start from the double bond (not from a carbon atom) and point to the H (or δ+ Br) atom. The second arrow in step 1 starts on the H–Br bond. A typical 3-mark answer: arrow from C=C to H and arrow from H–Br to Br; correct carbocation; arrow from Br⁻ lone pair to C⁺.

In the mechanism of HBr addition to ethene, where must the first curly arrow start?

  1. On a carbon atom
  2. On the Br atom
  3. On the C=C double bond
  4. On the H atom

The electron pair that forms the new C–H bond comes from the π bond, so the arrow starts at the double bond and points to the δ+ H.

R3.4.12 Unsymmetrical alkenes and Markovnikov's rule AHL

When HBr (or H₂O) adds to an unsymmetrical alkene such as propene, the H can attach to either carbon of the double bond, so two products are possible. They are not formed equally. (The problem does not arise for ethene, which is symmetrical.)

  • H adds to the end carbon (CH₂) → secondary carbocation CH₃CH⁺CH₃ → 2-bromopropane (major)
  • H adds to the middle carbon → primary carbocation CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ → 1-bromopropane (minor)
Key pointCarbocation stability: tertiary (3°) > secondary (2°) > primary (1°) > methyl. Alkyl groups are electron-releasing (positive inductive effect): they push electron density towards the positive carbon and spread out the charge. The more alkyl groups attached, the more stable the carbocation. The major product forms via the more stable carbocation, because it has the lower activation energy and forms faster.

Markovnikov's rule summarises this: when HX or H₂O adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen attaches to the carbon of the double bond that already has more hydrogen atoms. Examiners require the explanation in terms of carbocation stability; "Markovnikov's rule" on its own scores no mark.

Worked examplePredicting the major product. (a) But-1-ene + HBr: H adds to C1 (CH₂, two H) → secondary carbocation CH₃CH₂CH⁺CH₃ → 2-bromobutane (major). 1-bromobutane is minor.
(b) Hex-1-ene + HBr → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CHBrCH₃ (2-bromohexane).
(c) But-1-ene + steam (acid catalyst) → butan-2-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃, because the secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary one.
(d) 2-methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ + HCl → tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺ → 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.

Which species is formed in the mechanism of propene + HBr that leads to the major product?

  1. CH₃–C⁺H–CH₂Br
  2. CH₃–CHBr–C⁺H₂
  3. CH₃–C⁺H–CH₃
  4. CH₃–CH₂–C⁺H₂

H⁺ adds to the terminal CH₂, giving the more stable secondary carbocation CH₃CH⁺CH₃, which Br⁻ then attacks to form 2-bromopropane.

Which is the major product of the electrophilic addition of HCl to propene?

  1. ClCH₂CH=CH₂
  2. CH₃CHClCH₃
  3. CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl
  4. CH₃CH=CHCl

Via the secondary carbocation, Cl ends up on the middle carbon: 2-chloropropane.

Explain how three isomeric products can form when HBr reacts with but-1-ene.

H can add to C1, giving the secondary carbocation and 2-bromobutane (major), or to C2, giving the primary carbocation and 1-bromobutane (minor). C2 of 2-bromobutane is chiral (H, Br, CH₃ and C₂H₅), and the planar carbocation is attacked from either face, so 2-bromobutane forms as two enantiomers (a racemic mixture). That makes three isomers in total: 1-bromobutane and the two optical isomers of 2-bromobutane. (These are optical isomers, not E/Z isomers – the products have no C=C.)

3-methylpent-2-ene reacts with HBr. Explain why more 3-bromo-3-methylpentane forms than 2-bromo-3-methylpentane.

CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃: if H adds to C2, the positive charge sits on C3, which is bonded to three alkyl groups – a tertiary carbocation. If H adds to C3, the charge is on C2, a secondary carbocation. The tertiary carbocation is more stable (more electron-releasing alkyl groups), forms with lower activation energy, and Br⁻ attacks it to give 3-bromo-3-methylpentane as the major product.

title: Electrophilic substitution of benzene, and mechanisms in synthesis (AHL)
html:
R3.4.13 Electrophilic substitution of benzene AHL

Do now: what is special about benzene, and what properties might this give it?

All six C–C bonds are the same length (between single and double), because six π electrons are delocalised around the ring. This makes benzene unusually stable: it resists addition reactions and prefers substitution, which keeps the ring intact.

Benzene, C₆H₆, is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon (arene). Aromatic compounds contain a benzene ring; aliphatic compounds do not (they may be straight-chain, branched or non-aromatic rings). Benzene has a ring of six sp² carbons with a delocalised π system above and below the ring (bond order 1.5 for every C–C bond). The π cloud is electron-rich, so benzene attracts electrophiles. But benzene undergoes substitution, not addition: addition would destroy the delocalised system and lose its extra stability (about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ of delocalisation energy). In substitution, one H is replaced and the delocalised ring is restored.

Nitration of benzene AHL

Reagents and conditions: concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid ("nitrating mixture"), about 50 °C (higher temperatures give more than one nitro group).

C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O

The electrophile is the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, formed when sulfuric acid (the stronger acid) protonates nitric acid, which then loses water:

HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻   (or HNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + HSO₄⁻ + H₂O)

The guide says formation of the electrophile is not assessed, but you should know NO₂⁺ and the reagents.

Mechanism:

  1. A curly arrow goes from the delocalised π ring (start inside or on the circle) to the N atom of NO₂⁺. A new C–N bond forms.
  2. This gives a positively charged carbocation intermediate: one carbon is now sp³ and bonded to both H and NO₂, and the remaining four π electrons are delocalised over the other five carbons. It is drawn as a horseshoe (an incomplete circle, open towards the sp³ carbon) with a + inside. The ring has lost its full delocalisation.
  3. A curly arrow goes from the C–H bond of the sp³ carbon back into the ring. The H leaves as H⁺ (removed by HSO₄⁻, regenerating H₂SO₄, which is therefore a catalyst).
  4. The full delocalised ring is restored, giving nitrobenzene, C₆H₅NO₂, and H⁺.
Exam tipThe 4 marks are: arrow from ring to N of NO₂⁺; correct intermediate with + charge and horseshoe (not a full circle); arrow from C–H bond into the ring; products nitrobenzene + H⁺. Drawing a full circle in the intermediate loses marks. The general mechanism works for any charged electrophile E⁺: C₆H₆ + E⁺ → [C₆H₆E]⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺.

Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition with electrophiles?

  1. Benzene has no π electrons
  2. Substitution keeps the stable delocalised π system intact
  3. Addition would need UV light
  4. NO₂⁺ is a nucleophile

Addition would permanently destroy the delocalised ring and its extra stability; substitution restores it after the H⁺ is lost.

Which feature of the intermediate in benzene nitration is drawn correctly?

  1. A full circle with + inside
  2. A horseshoe open towards the carbon bearing H and NO₂, with + inside
  3. A neutral ring with NO₂ attached
  4. A radical with an unpaired electron

Only five carbons share the four remaining π electrons, so the delocalisation is incomplete: a horseshoe plus a positive charge.

Nitration is the first step in making aromatic amines (used for azo dyes) and explosives such as TNT (2,4,6-trinitromethylbenzene); nitration of methylbenzene follows exactly the same mechanism. Nitrobenzene is reduced to phenylamine with tin and concentrated HCl (then NaOH): C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] → C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O.

Reduction reactions in context

Reduction of organic compounds is assessed in Reactivity 3.2, but it links to R3.4 because the reducing agents (NaBH₄, LiAlH₄) act as sources of the hydride ion, H⁻, which is a nucleophile. The hydride's lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon of a C=O group.

  • Ketone → secondary alcohol: CH₃COCH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃
  • Aldehyde → primary alcohol: CH₃CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂OH
  • Carboxylic acid → aldehyde → primary alcohol (needs the stronger LiAlH₄): CH₃COOH + 4[H] → CH₃CH₂OH + H₂O
  • Alkene/alkyne + H₂ (Ni catalyst) → alkane: hydrogenation lowers the degree of unsaturation.

Mechanisms and names of specific reducing agents are not assessed; use [H] in equations.

Mechanism summary: which reaction is which?

MechanismSubstrate + reagentConditionsAttacking speciesBond fission
Free-radical substitution (R3.3)Alkane + X₂UV lightRadical X•Homolytic
Nucleophilic substitutionHalogenoalkane + OH⁻ / CN⁻ / NH₃Warm, aqueous (OH⁻)NucleophileHeterolytic
Electrophilic additionAlkene + HX / X₂ / H₂ORoom temp (H₂O: acid catalyst, heat)ElectrophileHeterolytic
Electrophilic substitution AHLBenzene + NO₂⁺Conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄, 50 °CElectrophileHeterolytic
Common mistakeBenzene → chlorobenzene is electrophilic substitution; ethane → chloroethane is free-radical substitution. Don't call any alkene reaction "nucleophilic addition" or "free-radical addition": with HBr, Br₂ and H₂O it is electrophilic addition.

Putting it together: reaction pathways

Give the conditions, equation and type of reaction for each conversion: (1) methane → chloromethane (2) ethene → chloroethane (3) chloroethane → ethanol (4) ethanol → ethanoic acid (5) ethanol → ethanal (6) ethanoic acid → ethanol (7) benzene → nitrobenzene
  1. Cl₂, UV light: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl; free-radical substitution.
  2. HCl, room temperature: C₂H₄ + HCl → C₂H₅Cl; electrophilic addition.
  3. NaOH(aq), warm/reflux: C₂H₅Cl + OH⁻ → C₂H₅OH + Cl⁻; nucleophilic substitution (SN2).
  4. Excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, heat under reflux: CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O; oxidation.
  5. Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distil the product off as it forms: CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O; oxidation.
  6. LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then dilute acid: CH₃COOH + 4[H] → CH₃CH₂OH + H₂O; reduction.
  7. Conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄, 50 °C: C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O; electrophilic substitution.

1.00 g of bromocyclohexane (M = 163.05 g mol⁻¹) gave 0.46 g of cyclohexanol (M = 100.16 g mol⁻¹) on warming with aqueous KOH. Calculate the percentage yield.

n(C₆H₁₁Br) = 1.00/163.05 = 6.13 × 10⁻³ mol; theoretical cyclohexanol = 6.13 × 10⁻³ mol = 0.614 g. Yield = 0.46/0.614 × 100 = 74.9%. (The other organic product, cyclohexene, comes from a competing elimination reaction.)

Green chemistry favours routes with fewer steps, higher atom economy, no solvents where possible and non-hazardous starting materials: less waste, lower energy use and safer processes.

Why understand mechanisms at all? (a 2-mark past-paper question) Knowing mechanisms lets chemists choose the best reaction for a target compound, predict and control the products, design new reagents and reactions, plan syntheses more effectively, and predict how changing conditions will affect a reaction.
